slides: Let's continue with this question, now with an estimate.

slides.say: [pause] Now the psychometric way, our third super-method, order-of-magnitude estimation. We used it already in the question with the root, when two hundred squared was forty thousand. Here we don't calculate the exact volume. We only ask how big it can be.
The volume of a cube is its edge length cubed. Three a times three a times three a. Three times three times three is twenty-seven, so the cube is twenty-seven a cubed.
The cylinder is inside the cube, so its volume must be less than the cube's. How much less? We don't know, and we don't need to. A part can't be bigger than the whole.
at: The cylinder is inside the cube

slides.say: Every choice is a number times a to the power of three. The cube's volume is twenty-seven times that same positive quantity. So we can compare the numbers in front of it. Pi is a little more than three. We'll use three to estimate those numbers.

Choice number one says twenty-seven pi over two, times a cubed. Twenty-seven times three is eighty-one, and over two, that's forty and a half. That's more than twenty-seven, so the cylinder would be bigger than the cube. That makes no sense, so choice number one is out.
at: so choice number one is out

slides.say: Choice number two says twenty-seven pi, times a cubed. Twenty-seven times three is eighty-one, three times the cube. A cylinder inside the cube can't be bigger than it, so choice number two is out.
Choice number three says thirty-six pi, times a cubed. Thirty-six times three is a hundred eight, four times the cube, so it's too big as well. Choice number three is out too.
Three choices make no sense, so we can mark choice number four.
at: so we can mark choice number four

slides.say: By the way, choice number four says twenty-seven pi over four, times a cubed. With pi as three, it's eighty-one over four, a bit more than twenty. That's about three quarters of twenty-seven, and that makes sense for a cylinder inside a cube.
at: By the way, choice number four

slides: Look at the choices they gave. Not three quarters, two thirds and four fifths of the cube, which would be hard to tell apart. They gave three choices that are each bigger than the whole cube. That's the exam's way of giving an advantage to whoever thinks. If you calculate the long way, it takes time, and you might slip. If you estimate, the choices help you.

slides.say: So when do I estimate? When the choices are far apart in size, and you can compare the answer with something you know, like the whole shape around it. Use a rough estimate, like three for pi here, to rule out what's too big or too small.

One more example. A circle is inside a square with side ten, and it touches all four sides. What's the area of the circle, if the choices are twenty-five pi, fifty pi, a hundred pi, and two hundred pi?

The square's area is ten times ten, a hundred, so the circle is less than a hundred. With pi as three, twenty-five pi is seventy-five, and fifty pi is a hundred fifty, more than the whole square. The other two are even bigger. Only twenty-five pi fits. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
